Snowflake does not allow non-SQL (Python/Java/Scala) UDFs to be CALLED inside a lambda passed to a higher-order function (`TRANSFORM`, `FILTER`, `REDUCE`, ...); the lambda body must compile to SQL. Spark allows any callable there. SCOPE - this applies ONLY when the lambda body actually invokes a registered UDF / `F.udf(...)` / `pandas_udf` object. A lambda built purely from `pyspark.sql.functions` expressions and column operators compiles to SQL and migrates unchanged, and nesting higher-order functions is supported; do not report this rule against such a site. In particular, `Cannot resolve variable '<v>' within lambda function` is NOT this rule - that is nested-lambda variable capture, which is fixable (see the higher-order-functions nested-lambda-variable-capture rule).
fix: First confirm a non-SQL UDF is really invoked inside the lambda; if not, this rule does not apply and the call migrates unchanged. If it is: lift the UDF out of the lambda so it runs over rows instead of over array elements - `F.explode` the collection, apply the UDF to the resulting column, then re-aggregate with `F.collect_list` / `F.array_agg` grouped back on the original key. If the UDF's logic can be expressed with SQL-compatible `pyspark.sql.functions`, inline that expression into the lambda instead. Only if neither is possible, annotate the site with the reason.

note: SCOS rejects GROUP BY <cols> GROUPING SETS (...) where the GROUP BY list is non-empty. Only a bare GROUPING SETS clause (without explicit GROUP BY columns) is accepted. Remove the explicit GROUP BY columns and rely solely on the GROUPING SETS specification.
fix: Remove the explicit GROUP BY column list; express grouping entirely through the GROUPING SETS clause: SELECT ... GROUPING SETS ((col1), (col2), ()).

note: SHOW TABLES / SHOW VIEWS / SHOW DATABASES / SHOW CREATE TABLE return Snowflake-shaped rows in SCOS (e.g. name, kind, comment, ...) instead of Spark's column contract. Code that accesses result columns by Spark names (e.g. row['tableName']) will fail. Use spark.catalog.listTables() / listDatabases() if the Spark schema is required.
fix: Replace spark.sql('SHOW TABLES IN ...') with spark.catalog.listTables(dbName) to get Spark-shaped results.

note: DESCRIBE TABLE returns Snowflake's schema shape (name, type, kind, null?, default, ...) in SCOS; the EXTENDED metadata section appended by Spark is not present. Code reading Spark-specific columns from the result will fail.
fix: Avoid parsing DESCRIBE TABLE output by column name; use spark.catalog.getTable() or SparkSession._jsparkSession for metadata instead.

note: CACHE TABLE / UNCACHE TABLE / CLEAR CACHE SQL statements are not implemented in SCOS — they have no equivalent on Snowflake and will silently fail or raise. Remove these statements; caching has no effect in SCOS.
fix: Remove CACHE TABLE / UNCACHE TABLE statements — they are no-ops on Snowflake and may raise in SCOS.

note: CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION SQL DDL fails in SCOS — SCOS forwards the SQL through sqlglot, but Snowflake requires different DDL syntax for UDF registration. Register the function at the Python level instead: spark.udf.register('name', fn).
fix: Replace CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION SQL with spark.udf.register('function_name', python_fn) in Python.

note: ALTER DATABASE is unsupported in SCOS — Snowflake does not support this DDL form via the Spark Connect translation layer. ALTER DATABASE SET LOCATION, SET DBPROPERTIES, etc. will fail at execution time.
fix: Remove ALTER DATABASE statements; manage database properties through the Snowflake native DDL or Snowpark Session directly.

note: Arbitrary table properties via TBLPROPERTIES (CREATE/ALTER TABLE ... TBLPROPERTIES(...)) are not supported in SCOS — the properties are rejected/ignored on Snowflake (FDN) tables.
fix: Remove the TBLPROPERTIES clause; set equivalent Snowflake table parameters via native DDL if required.

note: Writing the `binaryFile` format is not supported in SCOS — Snowflake's writer has no binaryFile sink. Persist binary content via a supported format (e.g. a BINARY/VARIANT column) instead.
fix: Replace .write.format('binaryFile') with a supported sink (store bytes in a BINARY column or stage file).

note: SCOS - pandas-list-to-stringtype: building a Spark DataFrame from a pandas DataFrame whose column holds Python lists/arrays (object dtype) and is mapped to StringType() in the schema fails under SCOS when the Arrow path is enabled (spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled, the Spark-Connect default). PyArrow infers the column as pa.list_(...) and SCOS has no list->StringType() coercion, so createDataFrame raises. Spark Classic's pickle path silently calls str() on each list, so the identical code runs in OSS Spark — this is a Spark-Connect-vs-Classic difference, not fixable in SCOS itself (SNOW-3590200). Workaround: pre-cast the list column to string before createDataFrame, e.g. pandas_df["value"] = pandas_df["value"].astype(str). Only applies when a pandas list/array column is ingested as StringType(); plain scalar columns are unaffected.
fix: Annotate above the call and pre-cast the offending column: # SCOS: pandas-list-to-stringtype - the Arrow createDataFrame path has no list->StringType coercion (SNOW-3590200); cast the pandas list column to str first -> pandas_df["<col>"] = pandas_df["<col>"].astype(str)

note: DataFrame.count() can hang/timeout on large datasets in SCOS; prefer SQL COUNT or avoid materialization in hot paths.
groupBy().applyInPandas(...) grouped-map pandas UDF; verify cloudpickle serialization and that referenced globals/broadcasts are accessible in SCOS.
mapInPandas(...) pandas iterator UDF; verify SCOS support and serialization.
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.extensions', ...) sets a STATIC config; SCOS rejects runtime modification. Configure via session params / packages instead.
spark.sql.shuffle.partitions has no physical effect on SCOS (Snowflake controls partitioning).
Iceberg time-travel via .option('as-of-timestamp'/'as-of-version', ...) may need the Iceberg extension; verify SCOS support.

dbutils.jobs.taskValues (Databricks Jobs task-value passing) does not exist in SCOS/Snowpark Connect — the dbutils global is Databricks-runtime-only. Pass values via explicit function arguments, a shared table, or environment variables instead.

SCOS already runs inside Snowflake — the `net.snowflake:spark-snowflake` connector (`write.format("snowflake")`) is not available in the SCOS runtime and is redundant. Write to a native Snowflake table instead.
fix: Replace `df.write.format("snowflake").options(...).save()` with `df.write.save_as_table("db.schema.tbl")` (or `.mode(...).saveAsTable(...)`).

note: Delta Lake format is unsupported in SCOS — the delta.tables module does not exist. Use Snowflake Iceberg tables or native tables instead.
Avro write format is unsupported in SCOS — Snowflake cannot write Avro files directly. Use Parquet or unload to a stage in another format.
Unrecognized Spark configuration key — most spark.executor/driver/memory/app configs are no-ops in SCOS. Verify the setting has an equivalent effect or remove it.
Datetime/timezone semantics differ between Spark and Snowflake for unix_timestamp.
Datetime/timezone semantics differ for from_unixtime.
Aggregation/window function percentile semantics differ.
printf/format_string semantics differ between Spark and Snowflake.
rlike/regexp engine differs (POSIX ERE vs java.util.regex).
JDBC source/sink behavior differs in SCOS (dialect coverage, options ignored).
com.databricks.spark.redshift data source is not supported in SCOS.
Observability API collect_metrics has no SCOS equivalent.
setJobGroup is a no-op in SCOS (no Spark UI/job groups).
Hive-style dynamic partitionOverwriteMode differs in SCOS.

The `SELECT * EXCEPT(col, ...)` / `col.* EXCEPT(...)` star-except projection (in selectExpr(...) or embedded spark.sql(...)) is Databricks SQL and is NOT part of the open-source Spark 3.5 SQL grammar. Because selectExpr()/spark.sql() parse their strings with Spark's Catalyst parser (even under SCOS), the EXCEPT(...) projection raises a parse error — this is a breaking change, not a behavioral difference. Distinct from the EXCEPT / EXCEPT ALL set operator, which is a separate supported construct.
fix: MUST rewrite. Replace the star-except projection with an explicit .drop() of the excluded columns. E.g. rewrite `df.alias("loc").selectExpr("loc.* except(Inserted_At, Inserted_By)")` to `df.drop("Inserted_At", "Inserted_By")` (drop the aliased-prefix and the EXCEPT list; .drop is case-insensitive and a no-op for absent columns, matching EXCEPT semantics). Do NOT leave the selectExpr EXCEPT form in the migrated code.

note: SCOS: when case-sensitive resolution is enabled (spark.sql.caseSensitive=True), dropGlobalTempView fails to resolve and drop global temporary views.

SCOS: the returned Database object's `description` is always None (PySpark returns the actual comment or empty string), and `locationUri` uses a Snowflake-specific `snowflake://<name>` scheme instead of the `file://` Hive warehouse path PySpark returns.
SCOS: listCatalogs (with no pattern or None) returns an extra `snowflake_catalog` entry alongside `spark_catalog`, whereas Spark returns only the default `spark_catalog`.

SCOS: the `description` field of returned Database objects is always None even when a COMMENT was set, and pattern matching differs — an exact name prefix without wildcards returns matches in SCOS but an empty list in PySpark.
SCOS: tableExists returns False for global temporary views referenced via the `global_temp.<view_name>` prefix, whereas PySpark returns True after the global temp view is created.

SCOS: dropping a nested field via dotted path (e.g. dropFields("d.e")) produces a flatter auto-generated column name than PySpark's nested-update name, and case-sensitive mode (spark.sql.caseSensitive=true) with a field name differing only in case diverges from Spark; the data result is correct but the schema column name differs.

SCOS: when `spark.sql.legacy.nullInEmptyListBehavior=true`, `Column.isin()` called with an empty list should return NULL for rows whose column value is NULL, but SCOS always returns false for those rows, ignoring the legacy null-propagation semantics.

SCOS: `Column.like` with a backslash escape in the pattern (e.g. `'%\%%'` to match a literal percent sign, `'%\_%'` for an underscore) returns no matching rows instead of the expected matches. The equivalent SQL LIKE predicate works correctly.

SCOS: `Column.withField` fails with a SQL compilation error when replacing a duplicate field name in a struct (Spark replaces all occurrences), and with a dotted path referencing an ambiguous field (e.g. `"a.c"` on a struct with multiple `a` fields) it does not raise the AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE_TO_FIELDS error Spark raises.

SCOS: with dict syntax (`df.agg({"col":"mean"})`) the output column is named `avg(col)` instead of `mean(col)` because mean maps to Snowflake's avg(), and floating-point aggregation results (avg/mean) come back with reduced precision (~7 significant digits) rather than full double precision.

SCOS: `DataFrame.approxQuantile` returns interpolated (continuous) quantile values that may not exist in the input data (e.g. 1.5 where PySpark returns 1.0), and on an empty DataFrame returns `[None]` instead of the empty list `[]`. Also: SCOS: the quantile approximation algorithm yields different numeric results than PySpark for the same input and relativeError (e.g. a median PySpark returns as 1.0 comes back as 1.5). On an empty DataFrame SCOS returns a list with one null per probability (e.g. [None]) rather than PySpark's empty list [].

SCOS: using `DataFrame.colRegex` as a column reference in a join condition raises an internal error instead of the expected AnalysisException, and self-join ambiguity detection via colRegex is not implemented (Spark raises an 'ambiguous' AnalysisException, SCOS does not).
SCOS: `DataFrame.cube` with an avg aggregation returns truncated floating-point results (e.g. 67.142857) instead of the full double-precision value (67.14285714285714) that PySpark returns.

SCOS: `DataFrame.dropDuplicates` with a column subset may retain a different row among duplicates than PySpark (which keeps the first row in natural order), so the non-subset column values in the result can differ.

SCOS: `DataFrame.fillna`/`na.fill` silently ignores a subset containing a dotted path to a non-existent nested struct field (Spark raises AnalysisException FIELD_NOT_FOUND), and in dict mode silently skips keys that are qualified/dotted column names, leaving those nulls unfilled instead of filling them.

SCOS: a no-argument convenience aggregation after groupBy (e.g. `.min()`, `.max()`, `.sum()`) drops all aggregate expressions and returns only the grouping-key columns instead of aggregating over all eligible columns. SCOS also does not honor `spark.sql.retainGroupColumns=false`, so grouping-key columns are always retained in `groupBy(...).agg(...)` output.

SCOS: a join condition referencing the same column on both sides (e.g. `df.a == df.a`) may include rows where the key is NULL, whereas Spark excludes them (NULL == NULL is FALSE), producing wrong results. LEFT SEMI and LEFT ANTI joins without an explicit condition also incorrectly raise an 'implicit cartesian product' error when `spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled=false`.

SCOS: when a `subset` column name contains dots and is backtick-quoted (e.g. `` `Col.1` ``) or uses a qualifier prefix (e.g. `alias.`Col.1``), `DataFrame.replace` raises an error instead of performing the replacement. Spark handles these column-name forms correctly. Also: SCOS: `na.replace` raises a column-not-found error instead of performing the replacement when a subset column name containing a dot is backtick-quoted (e.g. `` `Col.1` ``) or fully qualified with an alias (e.g. `` alias.`Col.1` ``); Spark strips the quoting and resolves the column correctly.

SCOS: when a column name contains non-ASCII or multi-byte characters (e.g. emoji), `show()` miscalculates the column display width, producing a narrower/misaligned column border than PySpark. The data is still displayed correctly; only the header alignment differs.

SCOS: when sort columns contain NULL values, `sortWithinPartitions` does not sort correctly — rows are returned in their original order rather than sorted. Spark places NULLs first for ascending and last for descending sorts with remaining rows properly ordered.
SCOS: calling `tail()` with a negative integer returns an empty list instead of raising the AnalysisException (INVALID_LIMIT_LIKE_EXPRESSION.IS_NEGATIVE) that Spark raises.

SCOS: unioning DataFrames whose struct columns were built from an expression alias (e.g. `struct(expr("id * 5 AS INNER"))`) yields an auto-generated struct field name (e.g. `col1`) instead of the declared alias. The union can also fail outright because Snowflake's case-sensitive struct-type comparison treats identically-named fields with different casing (or MAP-valued columns) as incompatible.

SCOS: when `withColumnRenamed` calls are chained so a later call names a column already renamed away by an earlier call, SCOS follows its internal rename-history and applies the rename, producing a different final column name. PySpark treats such a call as a no-op since the old name no longer exists.

SCOS: writing to a Spark temp view by name via `writeTo("view").append()` (etc.) raises a table-not-found error instead of writing to the view's underlying table, and the `.option("path", ...)` passed to `writeTo().create()` is silently ignored rather than directing output to a file-based data source.

SCOS: aggregating a FloatType column yields reduced 32-bit precision (e.g. 2.1 becomes 2.0999999046325684) instead of Spark's full 64-bit values, applying array_agg to nested/structured types fails with an internal execution error, and using it as a window function with a descending ORDER BY diverges from Spark.
SCOS: when either input array value itself is NULL (not just containing NULL elements), arrays_overlap returns False instead of the NULL that Spark returns.

SCOS: calling assert_true with a false condition and a null error-message argument (e.g. assert_true(col, lit(null))) silently returns null instead of raising a SparkException, because the internal error is raised via a SQL CONCAT that produces null in Snowflake and never fires.

SCOS: passing a non-BINARY column to bitmap_count does not raise Spark's AnalysisException (DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_INPUT_TYPE) at analysis time; the call is forwarded to Snowflake, which surfaces a runtime SQL compilation error instead.

SCOS: bitmap_or_agg raises a runtime SQL compilation error in complex multi-level GROUP BY aggregations (e.g. combining bitmap_bucket_number and bitmap_construct_agg sub-queries with GROUP BY ALL) that Spark evaluates successfully, and it skips Spark's type validation, so a non-BINARY argument does not raise the expected AnalysisException (DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_INPUT_TYPE).

SCOS: for a double only slightly above an x.5 midpoint (e.g. 0.500001, 2.500001), bround rounds down to the even integer (0.0, 2.0) instead of up (1.0, 3.0) as PySpark does, because the value is cast to Decimal first, losing the fractional offset and triggering banker's rounding toward even.
SCOS: the two-argument form ceil(col, scale) returns a DecimalType instead of the LongType Spark always returns, causing schema mismatches for callers that depend on the integer return type.

SCOS: `conv` raises an error when `fromBase`/`toBase` are column references (only literal integer bases are handled), and produces incorrect output for conversions whose result string exceeds 64 characters (large-value overflow diverges from Spark 3.5.x per SPARK-36229).
SCOS: `cosh` can differ from Spark by 1 ULP for some inputs (e.g. cosh(1.0) returns 1.5430806348152437 vs Spark's 1.543080634815244) because Snowflake's math library differs from Java's Math.cosh.

SCOS: `count_if` does not validate argument type — calling it with a non-boolean column (e.g. a string) raises no error or yields a Snowflake SQL compilation error, whereas Spark raises AnalysisException at analysis time. Ensure the argument is boolean.

SCOS: in SQL, when a table/view has a column named `current_date`, SCOS unconditionally treats the bare identifier as the built-in function (returning `date`) instead of resolving it as the column reference. Spark shadows the built-in with the column, so results silently diverge.

SCOS: `date_add` incorrectly accepts a BIGINT `days` argument and returns a result, whereas Spark raises AnalysisException (DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_INPUT_TYPE) because only INT/SMALLINT/TINYINT are allowed for that parameter.

SCOS: for dates beyond year 9999 (e.g. unix day 2932897 → year 10000), `date_from_unix_date` omits the leading '+' sign ('10000-01-01') that PySpark prefixes ('+10000-01-01'), a formatting divergence for out-of-range years.

SCOS: `dayofmonth` (and its alias `day`) fails at runtime when the argument is a timestamp produced by interval arithmetic (e.g. a string column minus a day-time interval), because the implementation wraps non-string inputs in to_date(), which cannot convert TIMESTAMP_LTZ to DATE. Spark extracts the day directly.
SCOS: `floor` with a scale argument returns a DecimalType instead of the Long/integer type Spark returns for that overload, causing schema mismatches for callers depending on the integer return type.

SCOS: when the extracted value is a JSON object, `get_json_object` returns keys in alphabetical order rather than original insertion order (a fundamental Snowflake JSON behavior), and JSONPath expressions with intermediate wildcards (e.g. '$.store.book[*].category') raise an error instead of returning the extracted array.

SCOS: with Snowflake extension behavior enabled, getbit accepts bit positions outside the valid [0, 63] range for a 64-bit integer and returns 0 instead of raising IllegalArgumentException. Spark strictly validates the position and raises for any out-of-range value.

SCOS: calling greatest() with zero arguments raises a Python 'list index out of range' error instead of Spark's AnalysisException. Code that catches AnalysisException for empty-argument validation will not catch it.

SCOS: the binary sketch from hll_sketch_agg uses a compact serialization format rather than PySpark's updatable (full) format, so the raw bytes differ even though the logical HLL sketch is equivalent. Additionally, on an empty DataFrame SCOS returns NULL instead of the empty-sketch binary value PySpark returns. Byte-level comparisons or downstream consumers expecting the PySpark wire format will break.

SCOS: the binary sketch from hll_union_agg uses a compact (space-efficient) serialization format, whereas PySpark returns an updatable (full) format with additional padding. The byte arrays differ although both represent the same HLL state and yield identical estimates via hll_sketch_estimate. Code that inspects or transfers the raw binary output will see different bytes.

SCOS: when ilike is given an invalid escape character (e.g. an integer literal or multi-byte string), it raises a generic SparkException wrapping a SnowparkSQLException instead of Spark's AnalysisException with error class INVALID_ESCAPE_CHAR. Callers catching AnalysisException for invalid-escape input validation will not catch the error.

SCOS: input_file_block_length is not supported and raises an unsupported operation error. There is no Snowflake equivalent for this Spark-specific physical file-metadata function (byte length of the file block containing the current row during a file-backed scan).

SCOS: input_file_block_start is not supported and raises an unsupported operation error, as there is no Snowflake equivalent for this Spark-specific physical file-metadata function. Rewrite to avoid dependence on file-block scan metadata.

SCOS: when the input JSON object contains duplicate keys, json_object_keys returns only unique keys, whereas Spark returns all keys including duplicates. For example '{"key1":1, "key1":2}' yields [key1, key1] in Spark but [key1] in SCOS.

SCOS: last_day is more permissive than Spark on non-standard date strings. For a format like M/D/YYYY (e.g. '1/3/1997') Spark returns NULL, but SCOS parses it and returns a valid last-day-of-month result, silently producing a value where Spark yields NULL.

SCOS: `locate` returns NULL for all rows when called via `selectExpr` with column-reference arguments (e.g. `selectExpr("locate(b, a)")`), instead of the correct positions. Additionally the 2-argument DataFrame-API form without a start position (e.g. `locate("aa", col("a"))`) raises an internal error.
SCOS: `log` with base `1.0` and a NULL column value returns Infinity instead of NULL, because the base-1 path returns Infinity without first checking whether the value argument is NULL.
SCOS: when `lpad` is given an invalid non-integer length string (e.g. 'invalid_length'), it silently returns NULL instead of raising Spark's [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] error.

SCOS: `make_dt_interval` truncates a seconds argument with sub-millisecond precision (e.g. 4.005006) to milliseconds (3 decimal places), whereas Spark preserves microsecond precision in the fractional-seconds component.

SCOS: when the ordering argument (second parameter) of `min_by` is a MapType, SCOS silently executes and returns a result instead of raising Spark's AnalysisException (INVALID_ORDERING_TYPE) at planning time, so it does not fail fast as Spark requires.

SCOS: `nanvl` raises a cast error when its first argument is a non-DOUBLE numeric type (e.g. INT or DECIMAL) instead of returning the second argument. Spark promotes both arguments to DOUBLE before the NaN check; SCOS skips promotion, generating a NaN comparison Snowflake rejects.

SCOS: `octet_length` returns different byte counts than PySpark for some types — 29 vs 19 for a TimestampType value, and the actual unpadded byte length of a CHAR(N) column instead of the declared fixed width N (including trailing-space padding).
SCOS: `overlay` on BinaryType columns returns garbled bytes rather than the correctly spliced byte array — all binary overlay operations produce incorrect results. String overlay works correctly.

SCOS: `pow` diverges from Spark's IEEE 754 semantics — `pow(-Infinity, 0.5)` throws an invalid floating-point operation error instead of returning NaN, and a NULL base with a NaN exponent returns NaN instead of propagating NULL.

SCOS: `product` aggregate returns floating-point precision errors because Snowflake has no native PRODUCT — it uses a log-sum-exp workaround (sign * exp(sum(ln(abs(x))))) whose exp/ln round-trip introduces IEEE 754 error (e.g. product(1..5) yields 119.99999999999997 instead of 120.0). Spark returns exact/correctly-rounded doubles.
SCOS: `raise_error` with a null message (e.g. raise_error(lit(null))) silently returns null instead of raising an exception. Spark raises SparkException in this case.

SCOS: a lambda compiled to Snowflake SQL can reference only its OWN parameters plus the parent dataframe's columns. SCOS holds the current lambda's parameters in a single slot that entering a nested lambda REPLACES instead of pushing, so an inner lambda that reads an ENCLOSING lambda's variable raises `AnalysisException: Cannot resolve variable '<v>' within lambda function` (SNOWPARK CONNECT ERROR CODE: 4001). Spark resolves the outer variable correctly. Nesting higher-order functions is itself supported, and an inner lambda may freely read a parent dataframe column or a literal - only capture of an enclosing lambda's variable fails, so it is the capture that must be removed, not the nesting. This is fixable without changing results: see `fix`.
fix: Pair the captured value into the inner collection in the OUTER lambda's body and read it off the inner lambda's own parameter, then unwrap if the inner HOF returns its input collection. Both steps, the constraints and the exclusions: references/python/nested-lambda-capture.md (Rule 32 of fix-rules.md).

note: SCOS: `rpad` with binary literal arguments in SQL produces the same computed values but a different auto-generated column name — SCOS renders binary literals in Python bytes notation (b'\x10 ') while PySpark uses uppercase hex-literal notation (X'1020').

SCOS: `size` always returns -1 for a null array or null map, ignoring spark.sql.legacy.sizeOfNull. With the Spark 3.x default (false), size on null should return null, but SCOS matches only the legacy (true) behavior.

SCOS: when a `soundex` input contains tab characters and does not start with a letter, the original string is returned; PySpark's show() renders such tabs as the escape sequence \t while SCOS renders them as literal tab whitespace. Values match; only display differs.

SCOS: `substr`/`substring` called with only two arguments (string and position, no length) names the output column 'substring(col, pos)', omitting the implicit default max-int length that Spark includes as 'substring(col, pos, 2147483647)'. This affects schema inspection and code relying on the auto-generated column name.

SCOS: `substring` called with only two arguments (omitting length) produces column name 'substring(c7, 2)' whereas Spark includes the implicit max length as 'substring(c7, 2, 2147483647)', causing a schema/column-name mismatch for two-argument invocations.

SCOS: `sum_distinct` on an integer column returns a Long result type, but Spark's Scala client expects a Double in certain contexts, so calling getDouble() on the Long result throws a ClassCastException.

SCOS: with base64 format and malformed input containing whitespace between padding characters (e.g. ' ab cdef= = '), Spark raises CONVERSION_INVALID_INPUT but SCOS strips whitespace and returns a decoded byte value, accepting invalid input Spark rejects.

SCOS: formatting float/double values with format strings that use '0' digit placeholders in the integer part (e.g. '0', '000.00', 'S000.') yields overflow indicators ('#') where Spark returns correctly formatted numbers, because Snowflake treats the floats with fewer significant digits. Integer types format correctly.

SCOS: with a 2-digit year format ('yy'), Snowflake resolves `YY` against the TWO_DIGIT_CENTURY_START session parameter (default 1970, so 00-69 -> 2000-2069 but 70-99 -> 1970-1999), while Spark always maps 00-99 to 2000-2099 — years 70-99 parse one century early with no error and no runtime EWI. Remedy: `spark.conf.set("snowpark.connect.use2000AsTwoDigitCenturyStart", "true")` once after the session is created; SCOS turns that into `ALTER SESSION SET TWO_DIGIT_CENTURY_START = 2000`, which covers every 2-digit-year parse in the session (all `to_timestamp*` / `to_date` / `unix_timestamp` forms and the same functions via `spark.sql`). Only applies when a format actually parses a standalone `yy` — `yyyy`/`yyy`/`y` map to `YYYY` and are unaffected. Literal formats are injected automatically by the `two_digit_year_century_window_config_rewrite` recipe; set it by hand when the format comes from a variable, config, or reader option.
fix: spark.conf.set("snowpark.connect.use2000AsTwoDigitCenturyStart", "true")  # once, after the session is created — only when a format parses a standalone 'yy'

note: SCOS: with a 2-digit year format ('yy'), Snowflake resolves `YY` against the TWO_DIGIT_CENTURY_START session parameter (default 1970), mapping 70-99 to 1970-1999, whereas Spark maps 70-99 to 2070-2099 — parsed one century early, with no error and no runtime EWI. Remedy: `spark.conf.set("snowpark.connect.use2000AsTwoDigitCenturyStart", "true")` once after the session is created; SCOS turns that into `ALTER SESSION SET TWO_DIGIT_CENTURY_START = 2000` for the whole session. Only applies when a format actually parses a standalone `yy`; `yyyy`/`yyy`/`y` are unaffected. Literal formats are injected automatically by the `two_digit_year_century_window_config_rewrite` recipe; set it by hand when the format is dynamic.
fix: spark.conf.set("snowpark.connect.use2000AsTwoDigitCenturyStart", "true")  # once, after the session is created — only when a format parses a standalone 'yy'

note: SCOS: a datetime *parse* format containing a standalone `yy` resolves the 2-digit year through Snowflake's TWO_DIGIT_CENTURY_START session parameter (default 1970, so 70-99 -> 1970-1999), while Spark maps 00-99 to 2000-2099. Years 70-99 come back one century early with no error and no runtime EWI. The century window is a property of the session, not of the individual function: `yy` is mapped to Snowflake's `YY` by one shared format mapping, so every member of this family — and the same functions called through `spark.sql(...)` — diverges identically. Fix once per session: `spark.conf.set("snowpark.connect.use2000AsTwoDigitCenturyStart", "true")`, which SCOS issues as `ALTER SESSION SET TWO_DIGIT_CENTURY_START = 2000`. `yyyy`/`yyy`/`y` map to `YYYY` and never consult the parameter, and formatting-only APIs (`date_format`, `from_unixtime`) are unaffected — rendering a 2-digit year does not read the century start. Literal formats are handled deterministically by the `two_digit_year_century_window_config_rewrite` recipe; a dynamic format (variable, config value, or a reader `timestampFormat`/`dateFormat` option) is invisible to it and must be set by hand.
fix: spark.conf.set("snowpark.connect.use2000AsTwoDigitCenturyStart", "true")  # once, after the session is created; do NOT repeat per call site

note: SCOS: the auto-generated output column name stays 'to_varchar(...)' instead of PySpark's normalized 'to_char(...)' (to_varchar is an alias for to_char), and float/double formatting with mixed '0'/'9' placeholders or PR/S/MI sign formats diverges from PySpark's output.

SCOS: when the format argument is a non-literal column reference rather than a string literal, trunc returns NULL for all rows instead of computing the truncated date. PySpark evaluates the format from the column value.

SCOS: when decrypting data encrypted with an explicit IV and AAD using an invalid or mismatched key, try_aes_decrypt raises a runtime error instead of returning NULL as Spark does on decryption failure.

SCOS: when a table/view has columns named after built-in date/time functions (e.g. current_date, current_timestamp), typeof resolves the identifier as the function call and returns 'date'/'timestamp' instead of the column's actual data type. Spark shadows the built-in with the column reference.

SCOS: passing a floating-point infinity value (float('inf')) to unbase64 produces different decoded bytes than PySpark, because the two systems convert infinity to different string representations before base64-decoding.

SCOS: when invoked from a SQL string via spark.sql(), SCOS resolves and executes unwrap_udt as a SQL catalog function, whereas Spark rejects this with UNRESOLVED_ROUTINE because unwrap_udt is a DataFrame-API-only function. SCOS accepts SQL usage that Spark would reject.
SCOS: user() returns the current Snowflake session username rather than the Spark/OS-level session user identity returned by standard PySpark, so the returned identity differs.
SCOS: xpath_long overflows on Long.MAX_VALUE, returning 9223372036854775808 (one above the max Long) instead of the correct 9223372036854775807, silently producing a wrong result for large values.

SCOS: when loading Hive-style key=value partitioned data, SCOS infers partition column types as StringType instead of the actual types from the partition values (e.g. a date partition comes back as StringType instead of DateType, and an integer partition as LongType instead of IntegerType).

SCOS: writeTo().append() targeting a temp view fails with a table-not-found error because SCOS does not consult the Spark session's temp view registry for write targets and treats the name as a missing Snowflake table. Spark resolves the temp view and appends to the underlying table.

SCOS: interruptOperation expects a Snowflake query ID as the operation identifier rather than a Spark operation ID, and the returned list of interrupted IDs likewise contains Snowflake query IDs. Callers must supply and interpret Snowflake query IDs, not Spark operation IDs.

SCOS: RDD.treeAggregate has no native RDD execution; rewrite as df.agg(...). The `depth` merge-topology arg has no SCOS analogue -- drop it. A non-identity zeroValue must be applied once (F.sum(...) + seed), not partitions+1 times. Workaround: see references/python/rdd-conversion.md 14.2.

SCOS: RDD.treeReduce -> df.agg(...) (degenerate treeAggregate; drop `depth`). Raises on empty in Spark but returns NULL on SCOS -- guard with F.coalesce or an explicit count()==0 raise; exact-integer products need F.round(F.product(...)).cast('long'). Workaround: see references/python/rdd-conversion.md 14.4.

Bounded by driver memory. Workaround: see references/python/rdd-conversion.md 16.5.
